The surface z = g(x,y) and the red point (2,1,2) are shown in the figure. Determine if the following directional derivatives g_{\vec{u}} \, (2,1) are positive, negative, zero, or do not make sense (because something is wrong with \vec{u}). Note: The directional derivative is also often written as D_{\vec{u}} \, g(a,b).
g_{\vec{u}} \,(2,1) where \vec{u} = (\vec{i} + \vec{j})/ \sqrt{2}.
g_{\vec{u}} \,(2,1) where \vec{u} = (\vec{i}-2\vec{j})/\sqrt{5}.
g_{\vec{u}} \,(2,1) where \vec{u} = (\vec{i}-\vec{k}) / \sqrt{2}.
g_{\vec{u}} \,(2,1) where \vec{u} = (\vec{j} - \vec{i})/ \sqrt{2}.
g_{\vec{u}} \,(2,1) where \vec{u} = -\vec{j}.
g_{\vec{u}} \,(2,1) where \vec{u} = -\vec{i}.
g_{\vec{u}} \,(2,1) where \vec{u} = 2\vec{i}+\vec{j}.
g_{\vec{u}} \,(2,1) where \vec{u} = (\vec{i} - \vec{j})/ \sqrt{2}.
